To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the scaling factor can be determined with a very high precision by measuring the spectral energy distribution and that the scaling factor is not ambiguous between up- and downsampling.

1) the spectral distribution of rescaled signals is a strong indicator of the exact scaling factor, 2) the spectral distribution is independent of the scaling factor in the case of upscaling, 3) the spectral distribution can be used to solve the ambiguity between upscaling/downscaling, and 4) the spectral distribution has a strong dependency on the scaling factor in case of downscaling.

(1) the spectral energy distribution (SED) of a resampled signal is not a function of the original image only, but also depends on the rescaling factor and (2) the SED of a resampled image can be used as a basis for inferring the scaling factor in a forensic setting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental problem of image forensics, namely, the estimation of the exact scaling factor from the image itself.
the following question: How to determine the scaling factor in the case of resampled images?
a novel forensic method for determining the exact scaling factor in resampled images.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presented work provides the first step towards a reliable forensic analysis of image scaling factors.
the proposed approach is a very promising tool in forensic analysis, which should be considered as a valuable addition to the forensic toolset.
the presented method is able to determine the correct scaling factor with high probability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to determine the exact transformation parameters of a resampled digital image.
we present a new method to determine the exact scale factor of resampled images.
we present the first passive and blind forensic approach to determine the exact transformation parameters of resampled digital image signals.
The main takeaway from our work is that

spectral methods for image scaling estimation are not only applicable to downscaling but also to upscaling, provided that a priori information is available on the spectral energy distributions of resampled signals.
spectral analysis is a viable approach to solve the scaling ambiguity and thus to infer scaling factors from resampled images.
spectral analysis of the rescaled image can be used to infer the exact scaling factor in a passive-blind setting.
